title: California Bans AI-Only Firing of Workers With Landmark No Robo Bosses Act
excerpt: Governor Gavin Newsom signed SB 947 on September 30, making California the first state to require a human to corroborate any termination or discipline decision driven primarily by AI — reversing his veto of a similar bill last year.
body:
• Governor Gavin Newsom signed the No Robo Bosses Act (SB 947) on September 30, 2026, making California the first state to bar employers from relying solely on artificial intelligence to fire or discipline workers.
  • When AI plays a primary role in a termination or discipline decision, a human reviewer must independently corroborate it using personnel files, manager evaluations, or peer reviews, and the worker must receive written notice plus a human contact for questions.
  • The law takes effect July 1, 2027, with civil penalties of up to $500 per violation, a private right of action for workers, and enforcement through the state labor commissioner or public prosecutors.
  • Newsom vetoed a nearly identical bill in October 2025 as overly broad; he signed this narrower version, authored by State Sen. Jerry McNerney, as part of a package of more than a dozen AI workplace bills.

California employers can no longer let an algorithm fire or discipline a worker without a person independently checking the decision. Governor Gavin Newsom signed the No Robo Bosses Act into law on September 30, the centerpiece of a package of more than a dozen artificial intelligence bills covering employment, surveillance, and health care. California is the first state to put a direct prohibition on AI-only firings into law.

Under SB 947, authored by State Senator Jerry McNerney, businesses may still use AI in human resources — but cannot treat algorithmic output as the final word. When an automated system is the primary driver behind a termination or discipline action, a human reviewer must corroborate the outcome using evaluations, peer reviews, and personnel files, and the worker must get written notice describing the data used plus a human contact.

Context & Background

The law is the product of years of union pressure and worker complaints about error-prone workplace algorithms. Labor groups describe systems that score employees, flag performance risks, and even recommend terminations — sometimes on faulty data or misinterpreted metrics. Lorena Gonzalez, president of the California Federation of Labor Unions, AFL-CIO, called it a direct response to worker demands.

This is not the first time the measure reached the governor's desk. Newsom vetoed a nearly identical predecessor, SB 7, in October 2025, writing that it imposed overly broad restrictions on how employers use digital tools. McNerney reintroduced a narrowed version in February 2026, stripping advance-notice requirements and dropping protections for gig workers, which blunted opposition from tech giants including Uber and Lyft. The Senate passed the revised bill in May; the Assembly cleared it later in the year.

The signing was part of a broader package: companion measures ban AI tools that read employees' emotions, prohibit surveillance in bathrooms, require disclosure when automation drives mass layoffs, and keep licensed medical professionals as final decision makers in clinical settings.

Impact & Analysis

The practical effect will hinge on a single word: "primarily." Employers that rely primarily on an automated system must now build human review into their termination workflows, document it, and maintain audit trails. HR software that scores workers and predicts flight risk is already widespread, and compliance teams will need to retrain managers on what adequate human oversight means — a rubber-stamp review will not satisfy the statute, according to employment-law observers.

Violations carry civil penalties of up to $500 each, on top of potential punitive damages and attorney's fees, with workers granted a private right of action. Enforcement runs through the state labor commissioner, the attorney general, or local prosecutors. None of it takes effect immediately: the July 1, 2027 operative date gives companies roughly nine months to rebuild termination workflows and renegotiate contracts with AI vendors.

Business groups warned of higher compliance costs; supporters counter that workers who fear opaque algorithms resist the tools entirely. Colorado and other states have introduced algorithmic-management bills, but none matches California's direct prohibition — and because national firms often adopt California standards, the law will likely shape HR practices well beyond state lines.

Diaspora Angle

California is home to the largest Indian diaspora population in the United States, heavily concentrated in the technology and services jobs where AI-driven HR tools are most widely deployed. For Indian immigrants and visa holders in the state's tech sector — many of whom already navigate precarious employment tied to work authorization — a law requiring human review before an algorithm can end a job adds a tangible layer of protection against opaque, automated management.

What's Next

Future regulations or court rulings will sharpen what "primarily relying" on AI means. Newsom used the signing to criticize the Trump administration's stance that the AI industry can regulate itself, framing California's action as filling a federal vacuum — a posture that sets up a state-versus-Washington fight over AI rules.
nri_angle: California's large Indian diaspora tech workforce gains a concrete safeguard against opaque automated firing and discipline decisions.
